question: Does the 2009 BFAR/NFRDI Northern Zambales assessment provide traceable regional marine fish evidence, and can its catch records be safely assigned to individual municipalities or present-day species distributions?

method.summary: Reviewed the complete official NFRDI-hosted Technical Paper Series PDF through browser text extraction, including its methods, study-area map, Figure 5, Tables 7, 8 and 10, summary, and references. No local PDF, image, table copy, raw landing records, coordinates, or voucher data were retained.
method.studyDesign: The report describes NSAP sampling from 1998 to 2002, with enumerators sampling fish boats unloading during daytime every two days, recording catch and species composition, and summarizing records by month and fishing gear. It says gear-specific fish identification relied on Allen and Swainston (1988) and Froese and Pauly (2000).
method.reportedCoverage: Northern Zambales marine fishery and landing catches. The abstract says work concentrated in Masinloc, Sta. Cruz and Candelaria; the methods name major landing sites in Subic, Masinloc and Sta. Cruz and a minor site at Candelaria. The report also says five of six observed sampling sites were in northern Zambales. Published species results are aggregated to the Northern Zambales area rather than cross-tabulated to individual capture locations.
method.reuseFinding: The PDF is publicly hosted by NFRDI, but no item-specific open license or reuse permission was identified in the reviewed publication. Public availability is not a reuse grant. No table, figure, or app publication is approved.

publication.title: Fish Stock Assessment in Northern Zambales Coast
publication.series: Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources / National Fisheries Research and Development Institute Technical Paper Series
publication.citation: Rueca, L. M., Bien, N. B., Bathan, R. M., Yuzon, J. I., & Salamat, G. B. (2009). Fish Stock Assessment in Northern Zambales Coast. BFAR/NFRDI Technical Paper Series, 12(3).
sourceLocators: Cover: series, December 2009, volume 12, number 3, and author list.
Printed pages 2-4: study objectives, stated limitations, sampling stations and 1998-2002 data collection.
Printed pages 10-12: species-composition figure and ten dominant species table.
Printed pages 13-15: tuna production and selected-species population parameter tables.
publication.accessStatus: Full official PDF reviewed via browser text extraction; no local copy retained.

sampling.samplingFrequency: Every two days, including weekends and holidays, according to the methods section.
sampling.sampleContext: Daytime boat landings; total catch and species composition were recorded. Production estimates combine monitored landing data and estimates for unmonitored sites, including interview-derived CPUE for minor gears.
sampling.gearAndLocationResolution: The paper reports fishery gear and landing stations, but the reviewed species tables do not give individual fish capture coordinates or a species-by-municipality matrix.
sampling.coverageDiscrepancy: The abstract's named focus omits Subic while the methods list Subic as a major landing station; the report also describes five of six observed sites as northern. Do not infer that every species row came from every station.

reportedSpecies.taxonomicTreatment: Names are transcribed as printed in the 2009 report. No current accepted-name crosswalk, specimen audit, or voucher check was completed; retain the source spellings and do not treat this subset as the complete 121-species roster.

reuse.licenseFinding: No item-specific open license or reuse permission was identified in the reviewed PDF.

internalConsistency.issue: The report's abstract lists Masinloc, Sta. Cruz and Candelaria as the concentrated study areas, while its methods identify Subic, Masinloc, Sta. Cruz and Candelaria as landing stations and the limitations section says five of six sampling sites are in the north.
internalConsistency.disposition: Preserve these source descriptions. Do not map regional species or catch totals to any one municipality or station.

internalConsistency.issue: The report says 121 species were identified, but the reviewed figure and selected tables expose only a subset of the names and no full machine-readable species-by-site catch matrix.
internalConsistency.disposition: Record only the 19 explicitly recoverable scientific-name labels, mark the roster incomplete, and do not present it as the complete Northern Zambales checklist.

internalConsistency.issue: The catch table values are raised historical fishery production in kilograms, not individual counts, standardized abundance, current catch rates, or site-level occurrence points.
internalConsistency.disposition: Retain the source metric and 1998-2002 period verbatim; do not use it for abundance or current catchability claims.

interpretation: This is a strong primary historical marine-fisheries source for fish species reported in Northern Zambales landings from 1998-2002.

The source is useful for research triage and historical regional catch context, but cannot establish present-day presence, exact capture location, safe or legal fishing, or availability at any named municipality.
Its scope is marine and fisheries-based; it supplies no river, lake, stream, or wetland inventory.
No fish occurrence rows, waterbody assignments, coordinates, legal or safety claims, or public-app data were added.
nextAction: Seek a newer, site-resolved Zambales fish survey or an independently reusable NSAP species-by-landing-site extract. Keep historical catches separate; verify taxonomy, site lineage, and reuse terms before any public species projection.
